memories-of-murder-2003.gazette: Ten women were killed around Hwaseong between 1986 and 1991, and the investigation ran on beatings, coerced confessions, and manpower that kept vanishing into civil-defense blackout drills. The film went out in 2003 with the case still open and the detectives still unnamed. In 2019 a DNA match identified a man already serving a life sentence for another killing; the statute of limitations had expired thirteen years earlier.

the-fog-of-war-2003.gazette: Errol Morris sat Robert McNamara in front of the Interrotron and then ran his answers against the White House tapes that had recorded him at the time. Kennedy's and Johnson's voices arrive as evidence rather than atmosphere, so the Secretary speaking to camera is cross-examined by the Secretary on reel. The arithmetic of the firebombing of Japanese cities — city by city, percentage burned — is delivered by the man who did the arithmetic.

downfall-2004.gazette: Two books hold the film up: Traudl Junge's memoir of her years as Hitler's secretary and Joachim Fest's reconstruction of the last days in the Führerbunker. Junge herself opens and closes the picture, in interview footage recorded shortly before her death in 2002. The underground chronology — the marriage, the poisonings, the surrender of the city overhead — is followed as documented rather than dramatized around.
downfall-2004.prism: Accuracy is the film's defense and also its problem: the more exactly the bunker is reproduced, the more a mass murderer gets to be a man having a terrible week. A faithful record still has to decide where the camera stands, and here it stands inside, with them.

head-on-2004.gazette: Hamburg's Turkish-German world arrives without the softening usual to migration cinema — psychiatric wards, bar-floor drinking, a marriage of convenience arranged so a daughter can get out from under her family's rules about her body. Akın breaks the story at intervals with a Roma orchestra on the Bosphorus, lined up and playing straight to camera. The Golden Bear went to a German film in 2004 for the first time in eighteen years.

moolaade-2004.gazette: Sembène was in his eighties when he took a crew to a village in Burkina Faso and built a film around 'purification,' the cutting still practiced across much of the region. Four girls run from the ceremony and a woman grants them sanctuary; moolaadé is the protection itself, binding on everyone who hears the word spoken. The village's confiscated radios end up burning in a pile in the square, which is where the film locates the argument.

grizzly-man-2005.gazette: Treadwell shot roughly a hundred hours of video across thirteen summers in Katmai, and Herzog built the film out of it after the bears killed Treadwell and Amie Huguenard in October 2003. The camera was running when they died, lens cap on, and the audio survives. Herzog listens to it on screen, in headphones, and tells the woman holding the tape to destroy it; the film never plays a second of it.
grizzly-man-2005.prism: The refusal is itself an edit. Herzog keeps custody of the one piece of record he says nobody should hear, and that withholding is what makes the rest of the footage unbearable — Treadwell filmed everything to prove he belonged out there, and the only reel placed off-limits is the one that proved otherwise.

pride-prejudice-2005.gazette: Joe Wright pushed the setting back to the 1790s, stripped out the powdered formality, and let livestock walk through the Bennet house. Hems drag in mud, hair comes loose, and the family is filmed as small gentry with a cash problem rather than as a heritage tableau. Purists counted the errors; the dirt was the argument.

the-child-2005.gazette: Seraing, the post-industrial steel town on the Meuse, has held the Dardennes' work since La Promesse, and L'Enfant stays put there: no score, no establishing gloss, the camera kept at shoulder height behind whoever is walking away. Bruno sells his newborn because someone in a stairwell will pay for it, and the film treats that as a transaction the town makes available. It took the Palme d'Or in 2005, the brothers' second in six years.

the-squid-and-the-whale-2005.gazette: Baumbach set the film in the Park Slope of his own adolescence and gave the parents his parents' professions — a novelist whose career is thinning, a critic whose career is starting. It was shot on Super 16 in about three weeks, in the neighborhood where the separation actually happened. The joint-custody schedule, down to which nights the cat changes houses, was the arrangement he grew up inside.
the-squid-and-the-whale-2005.prism: Writing your parents as characters means you get final cut on them, and the father takes most of the damage. The plagiarism subplot is the tell: the film knows that taking someone else's material and signing your own name to it is precisely the transaction it is running.

fireworks-wednesday-2006.gazette: The whole thing unfolds on the last Wednesday before Nowruz, with bonfires and firecrackers going off around a Tehran apartment block while a marriage comes apart two doors down. Farhadi hands the point of view to a cleaner hired for the day, a young woman about to be married herself, and never lets the audience know more than she does. Nothing is adjudicated at the end; the fireworks stop and people go home.

marie-antoinette-2006.gazette: Coppola shot in Versailles itself, on the palace's terms, then scored the dauphine's life with post-punk and slipped a pair of Converse into a shot of the shoe collection. The anachronism is the method rather than a slip: the court is read as a teenage court, sealed and bored, with a girl of fourteen shipped in to produce an heir. The film stops before the Revolution reaches her, at the carriage pulling away from the palace.

the-host-2006.gazette: In February 2000 a mortician at the US Army base in Yongsan ordered bottles of formaldehyde poured down a drain that emptied into the Han. The dumping was real and became a public scandal in Seoul; Bong opens the film with it, staged close to how it was reported, before letting the river produce something. The quarantine, the imported chemical agent, the family left to handle it alone — all of it runs on the logic set at that drain.
the-host-2006.prism: Making the spill the monster's origin means the monster isn't the villain, just a byproduct, and the people who produced it never appear again. The anger stays pointed at the response: the cordon, the misinformation, the chemical eventually sprayed on the citizens rather than on the thing in the water.

the-lives-of-others-2006.gazette: Donnersmarck worked inside the Ministry for State Security's own buildings and dressed the sets from Stasi stock — the cameras, the steamer for opening mail, the typewriters tracked by ribbon. Former officers were consulted on procedure, down to how long a man can be kept awake in an interrogation and how the scent samples were jarred and shelved. Ulrich Mühe, who plays the man in the attic doing the listening, had a file of his own from before 1989.

the-up-series-2006.gazette: It began in 1964 as a one-off for Granada: fourteen seven-year-olds selected across the British class system, filmed to test whether the Jesuit line about a child at seven would hold. Michael Apted, a researcher on that first program, has gone back every seven years since, and the footage now runs the length of the participants' adult lives. The people on screen are not characters — some have stopped answering the door, and the series records that too.

4-months-3-weeks-and-2-days.gazette: Decree 770 outlawed abortion in Romania in 1966 and stood for twenty-three years, enforced with workplace gynecological checks and birth targets written into the state's economic planning. Mungiu sets the film in 1987, near the end of that, and holds the camera still while the transaction is arranged: a hotel room, a stranger, a price that keeps moving. There is no score, and the law is never explained to the audience — it is simply the air in the room.
4-months-3-weeks-and-2-days.prism: The cost isn't the procedure, it's what the law leaves on the market: with no legal route, the only people offering help are people who can name their own terms, and the terms stop being money. Otilia pays the bill for a decision that was never hers, which is how a population policy actually gets enforced — one room at a time.
